items.title: Cursor ships Computer Use — agents can now click and type across any app on your computer
items.summary: Cursor's coding agents can now drive any desktop app, not just the browser. Cursor's own demo: an agent adds a "favorite trails" feature and tests it live in the iOS Simulator. Invoked automatically when a task needs it, or by @-mentioning Computer Use in a prompt.
items.why: An agent that can click through your actual UI to verify what it just built closes a real gap — until now you had to eyeball the result yourself or wire up a separate test harness.
items.action: Update Cursor, then @-mention Computer Use in a prompt where you want the agent to test a UI change it just made (a simulator, a desktop app, anything with no API) instead of describing it and hoping.

items.title: Claude Security now scans continuously and tracks fixes automatically
items.summary: Connect a repo once (GitHub, GitLab, or any Git provider) and Claude Security re-scans on every change based on risk and complexity, not on a fixed schedule. It builds an editable threat model per project, rates each finding's severity and exploit path, and closes findings automatically when a fix ships — reopening them if the issue comes back. $25K/month in free usage credits for two months.
items.why: Most scanners hand you a snapshot that goes stale the moment code moves; this one stays current with your codebase and tracks whether a finding actually got fixed, without someone re-running a scan.
items.action: If you're on Claude Enterprise, enable the Claude Security plugin for Claude Code (in beta for all Claude Code users) on one repo and see what its generated threat model gets right.

items.title: Elvis Saravia: plain RAG over raw chat history beats complex agentic memory systems
items.summary: A new paper's Raw-RAG baseline — just dense retrieval plus reranking over the unmodified conversation — ranks first in 6 of 7 benchmark/model settings against Mem0, MemOS and Memora, by 0.13 to 5.53 points, and ingests in 0.3 hours against 3.2–27 hours for the agentic-memory systems. Rewriting history into memory entries tends to drop the relations and dependency paths an answer actually needs.
items.why: Before you reach for a memory framework, it's worth knowing the fancier option sometimes loses to just keeping the raw transcript and searching it well.
items.action: Next time you're tempted to bolt a memory layer onto an agent, benchmark a raw dense-retrieval baseline against it first — on your own data, not the paper's.

eval.reason: Genuine new research finding with concrete numbers (6/7 settings, exact point deltas, ingestion-time comparison); not a duplicate of the 2026-10-23 MemoryTax item — different paper and benchmark, different angle (raw-RAG specifically beating agentic memory, not just beating full-context).

items.title: AWS's Kiro team: a system that watches Kiro's own runs opened 8 PRs in its first week, 7 merged, 0 bounced
items.summary: kiro-trace reads Kiro's own agent runs to find where it fails or wastes effort, proposes a fix, and keeps it only if deterministic checks and then a human reviewer accept it. First week: 8 PRs opened, 7 merged, 1 closed for unrelated reasons, none sent back in code review. One fix cut redundant file re-reads by about 83%.
items.why: A coding-agent team using its own run traces to fix the agent itself, gated by deterministic checks before a human ever reviews it, is a concrete harness-improvement loop — not just a roadmap promise.
items.action: If you're tuning your own agent harness, steal the pattern: mine your own run traces for waste/failure, let a model propose the fix, and gate it behind a check built to reject bad changes before a human sees it.

eval.reason: Genuine first-party account of a concrete self-improving-harness workflow with specific numbers (8 PRs, 7 merged, 83% reduction); not previously covered.

items.title: A one-sentence fix for coding agents that silently follow a stale CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md over your actual code
items.summary: Across 320 controlled runs on Claude Code and Codex CLI, agents followed a stale instruction file over conflicting existing code about 90% of the time — Claude Code noticed the conflict in 79 of 80 runs but followed the file anyway. Adding one precedence sentence to the user-level instruction file flipped that: following the code rose from 4.2% to 91.4%, and the test pass rate rose from 89.4% to 100%.
items.why: If your CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md has drifted even slightly from your actual codebase conventions, your agent is probably obeying the stale file over the code it can see — and a one-line fix mostly stops it.
items.action: Add a sentence to your user-level Claude Code / Codex instruction file telling it to defer to existing code over the project instruction file when the two conflict, then see if it stops rewriting working code to match a stale doc.

items.title: Is the Agent Harness Dead? — Jediah Katz, SpaceXAI
items.summary: Cursor's former longest-tenured agent-harness engineer, now at SpaceXAI, argues smarter models are absorbing what fancy harnesses used to patch in — but the harness matters more than ever for what models can't absorb: infrastructure, trust/security, and efficiency. Prediction: 90% of agent work runs off the laptop within six months.
items.why: A structured, research-cited argument on exactly the question harness-engineering work lives inside — what a harness is actually for once the model gets good enough to need less hand-holding.

items.title: Don't Trust Your AI Agents. Test Them Like a Scientist — Stephanie Jarmak, Omni Analytics
items.summary: A former astronomer turned eval-builder shows that swapping only the harness moved her results by 30% — same model, different wiring, different answer — and argues public benchmarks are for shortlisting, not decisions. Walks through designing your own evals like an experiment: realistic tasks, repeated runs, full traces, and a measurement that matches what you actually care about.
items.why: If you've ever trusted a benchmark number without checking whether it survives a harness swap, this is the talk that explains why that number might not mean what you think.
